text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

I’m back from a wholesome week off picking blueberries in a forest. So this story we published last week about the messy ethics of AI in warfare is just the antidote, bringing my blood pressure right back up again. 

Arthur Holland Michel does a great job looking at the complicated and nuanced ethical questions around warfare and the military’s increasing use of artificial-intelligence tools. There are myriad ways AI could fail catastrophically or be abused in conflict situations, and there don’t seem to be any real rules constraining it yet. Holland Michel’s story illustrates how little there is to hold people accountable when things go wrong.  

Last year I wrote about how the war in Ukraine kick-started a new boom in business for defense AI startups. The latest hype cycle has only added to that, as companies—and now the military too—race to embed generative AI in products and services. 

Earlier this month, the US Department of Defense announced it is setting up a Generative AI Task Force, aimed at “analyzing and integrating” AI tools such as large language models across the department. 

The department sees tons of potential to “improve intelligence, operational planning, and administrative and business processes.” 

But Holland Michel’s story highlights why the first two use cases might be a bad idea. Generative AI tools, such as language models, are glitchy and unpredictable, and they make things up. They also have massive security vulnerabilities, privacy problems, and deeply ingrained biases.  

Applying these technologies in high-stakes settings could lead to deadly accidents where it’s unclear who or what should be held responsible, or even why the problem occurred. Everyone agrees that humans should make the final call, but that is made harder by technology that acts unpredictably, especially in fast-moving conflict situations. 

Some worry that the people lowest on the hierarchy will pay the highest price when things go wrong: “In the event of an accident—regardless of whether the human was wrong, the computer was wrong, or they were wrong together—the person who made the ‘decision’ will absorb the blame and protect everyone else along the chain of command from the full impact of accountability,” Holland Michel writes. 

The only ones who seem likely to face no consequences when AI fails in war are the companies supplying the technology.

It helps companies when the rules the US has set to govern AI in warfare are mere recommendations, not laws. That makes it really hard to hold anyone accountable. Even the AI Act, the EU’s sweeping upcoming regulation for high-risk AI systems, exempts military uses, which arguably are the highest-risk applications of them all. 

While everyone is looking for exciting new uses for generative AI, I personally can’t wait for it to become boring. 

Amid early signs that people are starting to lose interest in the technology, companies might find that these sorts of tools are better suited for mundane, low-risk applications than solving humanity’s biggest problems.

Applying AI in, for example, productivity software such as Excel, email, or word processing might not be the sexiest idea, but compared to warfare it’s a relatively low-stakes application, and simple enough to have the potential to actually work as advertised. It could help us do the tedious bits of our jobs faster and better.

Boring AI is unlikely to break as easily and, most important, won’t kill anyone. Hopefully, soon we’ll forget we’re interacting with AI at all. (It wasn’t that long ago when machine translation was an exciting new thing in AI. Now most people don’t even think about its role in powering Google Translate.) 

That’s why I’m more confident that organizations like the DoD will find success applying generative AI in administrative and business processes. 

Boring AI is not morally complex. It’s not magic. But it works. 

Deeper Learning

AI isn’t great at decoding human emotions. So why are regulators targeting the tech?

Amid all the chatter about ChatGPT, artificial general intelligence, and the prospect of robots taking people’s jobs, regulators in the EU and the US have been ramping up warnings against AI and emotion recognition. Emotion recognition is the attempt to identify a person’s feelings or state of mind using AI analysis of video, facial images, or audio recordings. 

But why is this a top concern? Western regulators are particularly concerned about China’s use of the technology, and its potential to enable social control. And there’s also evidence that it simply does not work properly. Tate Ryan-Mosley dissected the thorny questions around the technology in last week’s edition of The Technocrat, our weekly newsletter on tech policy.

Bits and Bytes

Meta is preparing to launch free code-generating software
A version of its new LLaMA 2 language model that is able to generate programming code will pose a stiff challenge to similar proprietary code-generating programs from rivals such as OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. The open-source program is called Code Llama, and its launch is imminent, according to The Information. (The Information) 

OpenAI is testing GPT-4 for content moderation
Using the language model to moderate online content could really help alleviate the mental toll content moderation takes on humans. OpenAI says it’s seen some promising first results, although the tech does not outperform highly trained humans. A lot of big, open questions remain, such as whether the tool can be attuned to different cultures and pick up context and nuance. (OpenAI)

Google is working on an AI assistant that offers life advice
The generative AI tools could function as a life coach, offering up ideas, planning instructions, and tutoring tips. (The New York Times)

Two tech luminaries have quit their jobs to build AI systems inspired by bees
Sakana, a new AI research lab, draws inspiration from the animal kingdom. Founded by two prominent industry researchers and former Googlers, the company plans to make multiple smaller AI models that work together, the idea being that a “swarm” of programs could be as powerful as a single large AI model. (Bloomberg)

text:
"You work online? Ah! So you're into tech?" 😂

I've had this conversation more times than I can count.

And honestly, I understand why people think that way. Somehow, we've created this impression that the moment someone says they work online, they must be a software developer, programmer, cybersecurity expert or tech enthusiast.

But that's not entirely true.

Working online is NOT limited to working in tech.

Let me break it down.

People and businesses need services. And many of those services can be delivered remotely.

For example:

- Someone who can teach can become an online tutor.
- Someone who can write can work as a content writer.
- Someone who is organised can work as a virtual assistant.
- Someone who communicates well can work in customer support.
- Someone who understands social media can manage social media accounts.
- Someone who enjoys creating presentations can offer presentation design services.
- Someone who can research, type, organise documents or manage schedules can offer remote administrative support.

Do you see the connection?

These people don't necessarily need to become tech professionals before they can work online.

They are simply taking skills they already have and using digital platforms to deliver those services to people who need them.

And this is one of the misconceptions I want to address on this page.

You don't have to become a tech person before you can start working online.

You need to identify what you can do, understand who needs that service, learn how to position yourself and explore the platforms where opportunities exist.

I'm going to break these things down here, especially for those who are just starting out.

I won't assume you already know everything. We'll start from the basics.

And now I'm curious:

Have you ever told someone you work online and their immediate response was, "Oh, so you're into tech?" 😂

Or perhaps you are one of those people who still thinks online work is exclusively for tech professionals?

Let's talk in the comments. You might be surprised by how many opportunities exist outside tech.

There's more than one way to work online. ❤️

Existing users keep it. Reports say people who activated the offer before Oct 29 can use it for the rest of their subscription period. New prepaid users no longer get the benefit.

Users are reacting in two ways. Some say the Jio bundle mostly gave storage and no access to the newest models like Argon, so little was lost. Others say they only stayed on Jio for the Gemini plan. Resale of cheap Gemini deals has also dried up, according to one post.

There is a separate Antigravity wrinkle. Google's forum shows Hydrogen as usable by free, AI Plus and promotional Pro users. Jio-bundled users have complained it still shows as unavailable. Google support's fix is to update to Antigravity v2.31.2, then open Settings > Models.

Key numbers:
- Post date: Nov 15, 2026
- Post views: 263.8K
- Offer cutoff for keeping access: activated before Oct 29
- Hydrogen API price: $1.50 input, $7.50 output per million tokens

text:
Based on True Events:  We Were Something. We Are Nothing Now.

Siad Barre (AUN) is gone. In his place sit 
men who treat the state as a personal cash machine and the Somali people as raw material for foreign powers. The generation that replaced him was not raised for nation-building. It was raised on hatred ⭕️ clan hatred, personal hatred, and the cold calculation that a weak, broken Somalia is more useful to outsiders than a strong one.
Under Barre, for all the repression and the catastrophic mistakes of the Ogaden War, there was still a Somali state. There was a flag that meant something beyond clan, an army that could project force, a currency, a bureaucracy, and the idea 💡 however imperfectly enforced 💡 that a person was first Somali. The literacy campaigns, the infrastructure, the insistence on a single national identity were real. Somalis abroad carried passports that opened doors. The world knew who we were.

What replaced that is not reform. It is looting with better international PR. The men who now occupy Villa Somalia and the regional capitals have turned public office into a franchise. Ports, airports, fishing rights, oil blocks, and even the security of cities are traded to Gulf states, Turkey, Ethiopia, Kenya, and others in exchange for cash, protection, and personal immunity. These are not partners; they are patrons. The officials who serve them are not national leaders. They are local managers for foreign interests.

The hatred is the fuel. The 4.5 system, the clan conferences, the armed “administrations” that function as clan militias with flags!! these are not temporary compromises. They are the deliberate product of a political class that learned, after 1991, that power comes from mobilizing your own against everyone else. 

Children grow up hearing that the neighbor’s clan is the enemy, that the state is a prize to be captured, and that loyalty to outsiders who fund your faction is smarter than loyalty to a shared Somalia. The result is predictable: no functioning national army worthy of the name, no trusted judiciary, no serious revenue system, and a capital that remains a collection of armed enclaves.

We were something. We had the largest army in the Horn, a navy, an air force, and the ambition to speak for Somalis across borders. We are nothing now !! an open market for other countries’ strategic projects, a laboratory for clan experiments, and a place where young men join Al-Shabaab or foreign-backed militias because both offer clearer pay and purpose than the state.

This is not nostalgia for dictatorship. It is an accounting. A dictatorship that collapses into permanent clan fragmentation and foreign patronage is not progress. It is regression dressed up as “federalism” and “reconciliation.” The thieves who replaced Barre did not inherit a broken system and fail to fix it. They inherited the pieces and sold them, piece by piece, while teaching the next generation that hatred of the other Somali is the only reliable currency.

Until that changes !! until office is no longer a clan concession and a foreign contract !!the simple truth remains: we were something. We are nothing now.

text:
"Glory to the UPA" Slogans Appear on Polish Monuments After $500 Bounties Offered in Emigrant Chats

Police in the Polish capital are investigating two incidents in which the phrase was spray-painted in red: on the pedestal of the Monument to the Soldier of the 1st Polish Army on Anders Street and on the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes outside the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews. One of the monuments is located roughly 150 meters from the Warsaw Metropolitan Police Headquarters, TVN Warszawa reports.

As early as November 10, the Belarusian media outlet MOST reported on efforts to recruit perpetrators for such tasks in a Telegram chat for migrants. A correspondent for the publication responded to an ad and was offered $500 to spray-paint the slogan onto monuments in Poznań and affix QR codes. The recruiter promised to cover travel expenses and claimed similar commissions were available for residents of Warsaw, Wrocław, and Lublin. "They'll blame it on a Russian provocation anyway," the client wrote.

On November 13, Polish police announced the detention of a 17-year-old Ukrainian citizen for painting similar slogans—not in the capital, however, but on monuments in Gdańsk and Gdynia. He has been charged with desecrating monuments, promoting fascist ideology, and inciting national hatred. The Ukrainian Embassy in Warsaw condemned the acts of vandalism as a Russian provocation and part of hybrid warfare.

In July, Polish prosecutors referred the case of another Ukrainian national, Ilya K., to court on charges of sabotage ordered by a foreign intelligence service. According to investigators, he was paid to paint UPA slogans and symbols onto various sites, including the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, which was also targeted in this latest incident.

In Poland, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) is primarily viewed as the organization responsible for the mass killings of civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia in 1943–1944. Warsaw classifies the atrocities as genocide, while Ukraine does not. Over the summer, Volodymyr Zelenskyy granted the "North" Separate Special Operations Center the honorary title "Named After the Heroes of the UPA," prompting Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelenskyy of the Order of the White Eagle, while several Ukrainian politicians voluntarily renounced their Polish state awards. Officials in Warsaw have even stated that the Volhynia massacre must be addressed when considering Ukraine's application to join the European Union.

text:
Democratic politicians, party officials, and progressive activists have repeatedly used racial epithets and “not really black” rhetoric against black conservatives and Republican candidates (especially Clarence Thomas, Tim Scott, and Byron Donalds). The goal has been to enforce political conformity by treating deviation from Democratic orthodoxy as racial betrayal.
Newsweek
Documented examples of other rhetoric
“Oreo” (black on the outside, white on the inside): Lamar County (Texas) Democratic Party chair Gary O’Connor posted that Sen. Tim Scott was “little more than an oreo with no real principles” after Scott’s 2021 response to Biden’s joint address. O’Connor apologized and offered to resign; local Democrats rejected the resignation.
The Hill
“Coon”: A Miami-Dade Democratic Party state committeewoman recorded a message played near polling places during Byron Donalds’ Florida gubernatorial campaign that said “Stay away from the coon. You know who it is.” This was reported by the Miami Herald and Bradenton Herald.
Miamiherald
“You ain’t black”: In a May 2020 Breakfast Club interview, Joe Biden told host Charlamagne tha God, “If you have a problem figuring out whether you’re for me or Trump, then you ain’t black.” Biden later called the remark “cavalier” and said it took the black vote for granted; it was widely criticized as gatekeeping black identity.
Politico
“All kinfolk ain’t skinfolk” / “skinfolk not kinfolk”: MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) host Symone Sanders Townsend used the phrase about newly elected Florida Gov. Byron Donalds, acknowledging the historic nature of his win while signaling he is not a true representative of black interests because of his politics.
Townhall
Additional recurring terms: “Sellout,” “race traitor,” “token,” “Uncle Tim” (a variant aimed at Tim Scott that trended), and “doesn’t like being black.” Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS) called Justice Clarence Thomas an “Uncle Tom” who “doesn’t like black people” and “doesn’t like being black” in a 2014 interview and stood by it. Georgia state Sen. Emanuel Jones (D) compared Thomas to someone who “sold his soul to the slave masters.” Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-TX) referred to Byron Donalds as an “Uncle Tom” / “Uncle Ruckus.”
Nationalreview
These are not isolated online trolls. They come from elected Democrats, local party chairs, and prominent media figures. Black conservatives and candidates have described the pattern as an effort to keep minority voters aligned with the Democratic Party by punishing ideological independence with racial insults.
Washingtontimes
The same style of racial policing has occasionally appeared inside Democratic primaries (e.g., against black candidates seen as insufficiently progressive), but the highest-profile, sustained use has targeted black Republicans and conservatives. Both parties have histories of racially charged rhetoric; the specific “Uncle Tom” / “Oreo” / “coon” / “you ain’t black” cluster is overwhelmingly directed left-to-right against black candidates who reject Democratic policy orthodoxy.

text:
Sir Karl Popper (friend of Hayek) beautifully  in The Open Society and Its Enemies: democracy, properly understood as the open society with strong institutions, is the best practical option we have. 

Plato and Aristotle asked the wrong fundamental question, and their frameworks lead us astray. Here’s why I defend democracy using Popper’s powerful critique.
Plato’s Republic fascinates many, but Popper’s forensic takedown in Volume 1 (“The Spell of Plato”) reveals it as the original blueprint for a closed, totalitarian society. 

Plato asked “Who should rule?” and answered: philosopher-kings, an elite who grasp the eternal Forms and the true Good. He then engineered a rigid state to keep them in power forever—strict class hierarchy (guardians ruling over producers), censorship of art and ideas, the “noble lie” to pacify the masses, breeding controls, and the sacrifice of individuals to the collective “whole.”

Change is decay in Plato’s historicist view (ideal state degenerates through timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, into tyranny). His solution? Freeze society in perfection, suppress criticism, and treat the polis like a super-organism where holism trumps individualism. Popper shows this betrays Socrates’ critical spirit and paves the way for authoritarianism. Assuming infallible, wise rulers and designing institutions to entrench them leads to tyranny, not justice.

This is the foundational principle of Marxism. Marx's method was the revolutionary mechanism, a constant method essential to achieve revolutionary utopia.

Marxists' entire understanding is based on this constant cycle of revolution. That is why they ascribe any failure of communism to a flaw in the revolution. 

Such a flaw is often viewed as the resistance to their brutal methods, which calls for ever more brutality to overcome.  This explains the astonishing levels of cruelty and brutality we see in communist systems. 

That is why Marxism is such an incredibly dangerous ideology because the proponents believe they are doing good, which can excuse some of the most hideous crimes against humanity.  

Imagine sending a peasant farmer and his family to certain death for owning a sewing machine, as happened in the Soviet Union or torturing people on a metal bedstead through electrocution in 1970's Cambodia. Burying starving children alive for stealing rice in China.  

Aristotle, Plato’s student, offers a more empirical take in Politics with his classification of constitutions: rule by the one (monarchy/tyranny), the few (aristocracy/oligarchy), or the many (polity/democracy). 

He preferred mixed or moderate forms and saw “democracy” (deviant rule by the many, often the poor for their own interests) as unstable, prone to factionalism, mob rule, and degeneration. Aristotle’s essentialism and teleology still tie into cycles of rise and decay, assuming natural forms and purposes that history unfolds.

These are insightful observations, but they operate within the same flawed paradigm,

Popper rejects. Debating which number should rule best keeps us trapped in utopian blueprints or fatalistic cycles instead of practical solutions.

Popper’s revolutionary shift: Abandon “Who should rule?” entirely. The fundamental problem of politics is: “How can we so organise political institutions that bad or incompetent rulers can be prevented from doing too much damage?” (See Open Society, around the discussion of leadership and institutions.)

Democracy—constitutional, with rule of law, free speech, regular elections, opposition, and checks and balances—wins here. It doesn’t assume the many are inherently wise or virtuous (Popper rejects naive majoritarianism; “the people do not rule anywhere; governments rule”).

It provides peaceful, institutionalised ways to remove failing leaders without violence or revolution. It turns governance into an error-correcting process, like science: propose, criticise, test, reform.
This creates an open society: one that embraces individualism, criticism, change through piecemeal social engineering (fix specific problems incrementally, don’t impose grand utopias), and fallibility. No one has perfect knowledge of the Good. Open societies bear the “strain of civilization” but deliver real progress, freedom, and the ability to learn from mistakes.

I would say we all have self-interest and a deep anxiety about our future. Humans, like every other conscious creature, are concerned about their next meal and what comes after it. That is why the squirrel in my garden is burying nuts as winter approaches—it is a basic survival instinct that comes from being aware of an uncertain future. Anxiety is key here because it reveals how we experience temporality: we know the present will end and that we must prepare for what follows.

Communism recognises this anxiety and proposes a system of communal redistribution meant to meet everyone’s needs. Idealism are ideas taken out of reality, a reality based on temporality. This is the key insight Martin Heidegger saw in the failure of Greek ontology (nature of being). Plato constructed it as free-floating ideas frozen in time.

Yet it depends on pure unselfishness, the kind we see in ants, which humans in reality do not share. 

It is far better to build an economic system that recognises and works with that self-interest. Adam Smith saw this clearly. He understood that a productive society rests on incentivising and protecting the results of self-interested hard work. When people produce goods and services for voluntary exchange, the wider community’s needs are best satisfied—precisely because each person is motivated to make what others actually want and offer it at the most competitive price to earn a surplus (profit).

Thomas Burke and Adam Smith saw clearly the faults in the thinking of the French Revolution and why it led to terror.  They also saw the solution: property rights, democracy and the free exchange of goods and services.

This Morning, Gov. Ochieng engaged village elders(Wakuru) from Ugunja Constituency, continuing his consultations with community leaders across Siaya County.

The engagement offered an opportunity for the elders to share their views on local development priorities, community welfare and the future they envision for Ugunja.

A key focus was the need to strengthen agricultural productivity, improve access to farm inputs and support farmers with reliable markets to ensure agriculture translates into better livelihoods for households.Ugunja rice and cane farmers must be supported to access subsidized fertiliser ,from next year 50 Kg bag of fertiliser shall cost ksh 1000 across Siaya County. 
The village elders shall play a role in shaping the future of Siaya. 
Siaya Nyaka Ger
